children.name: Taeniopygia
children.description: The zebra finches — a small genus of Australasian estrildids known for their distinctively patterned plumage and remarkable adaptability to arid environments. The Zebra Finch is one of the most studied songbirds in laboratory research, particularly in neurobiology, learning, and vocal communication. They are social, gregarious birds that form enormous flocks in suitable habitat.

children.name: Taeniopygia guttata
children.description:
The Sunda zebra finch (Taeniopygia guttata) is a species of bird in the family Estrildidae. It is found in the Lesser Sundas. For almost two centuries, its closest relative from Australia was generally included in T.guttata as a subspecies; since the 2020s it is generally considered a separate species Taeniopygia castanotis.
Most pre-2020 literature referencing "T.guttata" actually refers to the birds now known as T.castanotis - in particular physiological, neurological and behavioral studies generally used "T.guttata" for the Australian species, because T.guttata sensu stricto was never kept in captivity in significant numbers, and thus was unavailable for such research.

children.name: Padda
children.description: The Java sparrows — a small genus of stocky, large-billed estrildids native to islands of Southeast Asia. They are notable for their thick, conical bills adapted for husking rice and other grains. The Java Sparrow has been a popular cage bird in Asia for centuries, which has led to extensive introductions across the tropics. They are highly social and often roost in large communal groups.

children.name: Padda oryzivora
children.description: The Java sparrow (Padda oryzivora; syn.

children.name: Padda fuscata
children.description: The Timor sparrow (Padda fuscata), also known as Timor dusky sparrow, is a small passerine bird.

children.name: Erythrura
children.description: The parrotfinches — a genus of brightly coloured estrildids with green, red, and blue plumage that give them a parrot-like appearance. They are found from Southeast Asia to the Pacific islands, with the highest diversity in New Guinea. Their stout, curved bills are adapted for feeding on grass seeds, figs, and bamboo seeds. Many species are prized in aviculture.

children.name: Erythrura gouldiae
children.description: The Gouldian finch (Chloebia gouldiae), also known as the Gould's finch or the rainbow finch, is a colourful passerine bird that is native to Australia.

children.name: Erythrura psittacea
children.description:
The red-throated parrotfinch (Erythrura psittacea) is a species of estrildid finch found in New Caledonia. It has an estimated global extent of occurrence of 20,000 to 50,000 km2.
It is found in both subtropical or tropical moist lowland forest and shrubland habitats. The IUCN has classified the species as being of least concern.

children.name: Erythrura pealii
children.description: The Fiji parrotfinch (Erythrura pealii) is a species of estrildid finch endemic to Fiji that was formerly considered to be a subspecies of the red-headed parrotfinch.

children.name: Erythrura kleinschmidti
children.description: The pink-billed parrotfinch (Erythrura kleinschmidti) is a species of estrildid finch found on the island of Viti Levu, Fiji. Commonly found at undisturbed mature forest in the centre and east of Viti Levu, e.g. Joske's Thumb near Suva. This species is found at mid-height along tree-trunks and branches, usually alone or in pairs but also joining mixed-species flocks, feeding primarily on insects, but also on flower buds and fruits.

children.name: Erythrura prasina
children.description:
The pin-tailed parrotfinch (Erythrura prasina) is a common species of estrildid finch found in Southeast Asia: Malaysia, Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Burma, Vietnam, Thailand and China. It has an estimated global extent of occurrence of 10,000,000 km2.
It is found in subtropical/tropical in both montane and lowland moist forest, and is also found in bamboo thickets and rice plantations. Flocks of this species can do great damage to rice crops, and in parts of its range it is classed as a pest. The IUCN has classified the species as being of least concern. It is a popular cage bird.

children.name: Erythrura hyperythra
children.description: The tawny-breasted parrotfinch (Erythrura hyperythra) is a species of estrildid finch found in Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines. It is found in tropical montane moist forests, grassy clearings and forest edges. The IUCN has classified the species as being of least concern.

children.name: Erythrura tricolor
children.description: The tricolored parrotfinch (Erythrura tricolor) is a species of estrildid finch found in Timor and the southern Moluccas.

children.name: Erythrura papuana
children.description: The Papuan parrotfinch (Erythrura papuana) is a common species of estrildid finch found in New Guinea.

children.name: Erythrura regia
children.description: The royal parrotfinch (Erythrura regia) is a species of estrildid finch endemic to Vanuatu in the South Pacific Ocean.

children.name: Erythrura cyaneovirens
children.description:
The red-headed parrotfinch (Erythrura cyaneovirens) is a common species of estrildid finch found in the Samoan Islands. It has an estimated global extent of occurrence of 20,000 to 50,000 km2.
It is found in subtropical/tropical lowland moist forest.

children.name: Lonchura
children.description: The munias and mannikins — a large genus of seed-eating estrildids distributed across Africa, Asia, and Australasia. They are stout, typically brown or black seedeaters with conical bills, often with contrasting white or dark heads and bellies. Highly gregarious, they form noisy flocks in grasslands and rice paddies. Several species have been domesticated and are popular cage birds, including the Society Finch.

children.name: Lonchura domestica
children.description: A domesticated finch derived from the White-rumped Munia through centuries of selection in Japan and China. It is not found in the wild but exists only in captivity, where it is known for its gregarious, non-aggressive temperament and free-breeding habits. Its varied colour morphs include chocolate, pied, and fawn. It is often used as a foster parent for other estrildids in aviculture.

children.name: Lonchura punctulata
children.description:
The scaly-breasted munia or spotted munia (Lonchura punctulata), known in the pet trade as nutmeg mannikin or spice finch, is a sparrow-sized estrildid finch native to tropical Asia. A species of the genus Lonchura, it was formally described and named by Carl Linnaeus in 1758. Its name is based on the distinct scale-like feather markings on the breast and belly. The adult is brown above and has a dark conical bill. The species has 11 subspecies across its range, which differ slightly in size and colour.
This munia eats mainly grass seeds apart from berries and small insects. They forage in flocks and communicate with soft calls and whistles. The species is highly social and may sometimes roost with other species of munias. This species is found in tropical plains and grasslands. Breeding pairs construct dome-shaped nests using grass or bamboo leaves.

children.name: Lonchura malacca
children.description: The tricoloured munia (Lonchura malacca) is an estrildid finch, native to Bangladesh, India, Sri Lanka, Pakistan, and southern China.

children.name: Lonchura atricapilla
children.description: | image_caption = Adult | image2 = | image2_caption = Juvenile both L.

children.name: Lonchura ferruginosa
children.description: The white-capped munia (Lonchura ferruginosa) is a species of estrildid finch found in Java and Bali. It is found in marshes, swamps, fens, grasslands habitat. The status of the species is evaluated as Least Concern.

children.name: Lonchura molucca
children.description: The black-faced munia (Lonchura molucca) is a species of estrildid finch found in Indonesia and East Timor. It occurs in a wide range of habitats including artificial landscapes (e.g. Parks and gardens), forest, grassland and savannah. It was first described by the Swedish naturalist Carl Linnaeus in the twelfth edition of his Systema Naturae in 1766. The IUCN has evaluated the status of this bird as being of least concern.

children.name: Lonchura caniceps
children.description: The grey-headed mannikin or grey-headed munia (Lonchura caniceps) is a species of estrildid finch, native to the Papuan Peninsula. It has an estimated global extent of occurrence of 50,000 to 100,000 km2. It is found in moist savanna, shrubland & wetlands. The status of the species is evaluated as Least Concern.

children.name: Lonchura vana
children.description: The grey-banded mannikin (Lonchura vana), or grey-banded munia, is a species of estrildid finch known to be found in Anggi Gigi, Tamrau Mountains, and Arfak Mountains in the Vogelkop Peninsula in north-western Papua, Indonesia. This species inhabits mid-mountain wet grassland and marshland. It also can be found on abandoned agricultural plots near human settlements.

children.name: Lonchura grandis
children.description: The great-billed mannikin or grand munia (Lonchura grandis) is a species of estrildid finch found in northern and eastern New Guinea. It is found in wetlands habitat. The status of the species is evaluated as Least Concern.

children.name: Lonchura castaneothorax
children.description: The chestnut-breasted mannikin (Lonchura castaneothorax), also known as the chestnut-breasted munia or bully bird (in Australia), is a small brown-backed munia with a black face and greyish crown and nape. It has a broad ferruginous breast bar above a white belly. The species' natural range includes Australia, Indonesia, and Papua New Guinea. It has also been introduced to French Polynesia and New Caledonia.

children.name: Lonchura leucogastra
children.description: The white-bellied munia (Lonchura leucogastra) is a species of estrildid finch. It is found in Malesia. Its natural habitat is subtropical/ tropical lowland moist forest habitat, and it is also found in grasslands and residential areas. The status of the species is evaluated as Least Concern. It is an invasive species.

children.name: Lonchura quinticolor
children.description: The five-colored munia (Lonchura quinticolor) is a common species of estrildid finch found in the Lesser Sunda Islands. It inhabits many different habitats even in artificial landscapes, forest, shrubland and wet grassland habitats. The status of the species is evaluated as Least Concern.

children.name: Lonchura striata
children.description:
The white-rumped munia (Lonchura striata) or white-rumped mannikin, sometimes called striated finch in aviculture, is a small passerine bird from the family of waxbill "finches" (Estrildidae). These are not close relatives of the true finches (Fringillidae) or true sparrows (Passeridae).
It is native to tropical continental Asia and some adjacent islands, and has been naturalized in some parts of Japan. Its domesticated descendant, the society finch or Bengalese finch, is found worldwide as a pet and a biological model organism.

children.name: Lonchura kelaarti
children.description: The black-throated munia or Jerdon's mannikin (Lonchura kelaarti) is a small passerine bird. This estrildid finch is a resident breeding bird in the hills of southwest India, the Western Ghats, Eastern Ghats and Sri Lanka.

children.name: Lonchura maja
children.description: The white-headed munia (Lonchura maja) is a small passerine bird belonging to the estrildid finch family. This species is often confused, and referred to as, the Pale-headed munia (Lonchura pallida) which can be differentiated by tan coloured flanks which are lighter than the brown wings and also by the absence of the black belly.

children.name: Lonchura pallida
children.description: The pale-headed munia (Lonchura pallida) is a species of estrildid finch native to eastern Indonesia and Timor-Leste. It inhabits subtropical and tropical lowlands, dry shrubland, grassland, marshes and agricultural areas. The species has shown recent range expansion due to increasing agriculture and land clearance. It has recently crossed the Wallace Line to establish breeding populations on Nusa Penida, and is now recorded on Bali. It has also become an increasingly frequent vagrant in northwestern Australia from the 2020s onward, with arrivals likely aided by monsoon winds and cyclones.

children.name: Lonchura stygia
children.description: The black mannikin (Lonchura stygia) or black munia, is a species of estrildid finch found in New Guinea, from Mandum (Papua, formerly known as Irian Jaya, Indonesia) to Lake Daviumbu, Papua New Guinea.

children.name: Lonchura teerinki
children.description: The black-breasted mannikin (Lonchura teerinki), also known as black-breasted munia, is a species of estrildid finch endemic to West Papua, Indonesia. It has an estimated global extent of occurrence of 20,000 to 50,000 km2. It is found in subtropical/ tropical lowland dry shrubland and high altitude grassland habitat. The status of the species is Least Concern.

children.name: Lonchura montana
children.description:
The western alpine mannikin (Lonchura montana) also known as Snow Mountain mannikin or western alpine munia is a small, approximately 11.5 cm long, estrildid finch. Both sexes are similar with dark brown plumage, black face, buff chest and black-barred white abdomen. The young has black bill, dark brown plumage and buffy-white below.
Endemic to Indonesia, the western alpine mannikin is distributed in alpine grassland of the Snow Mountains and Star Mountains in western New Guinea. It usually found in flocks of six to twenty birds. The diet consists mainly of seeds, grasses and other vegetation.

children.name: Lonchura spectabilis
children.description: The hooded mannikin or hooded munia (Lonchura spectabilis), also known as the New Britain mannikin or Sclater's mannikin, is a species of estrildid finch found in New Britain and New Guinea.

children.name: Lonchura nevermanni
children.description:
The grey-crowned mannikin (Lonchura nevermanni), or grey-crowned munia, is a species of estrildid finch of southern New Guinea. It has an estimated global extent of occurrence of 20,000 to 50,000 km2.
It is found in moist savanna & wetlands habitats. The status of the species is evaluated as Least Concern.

children.name: Lonchura hunsteini
children.description: Mottled mannikin or mottled munia (Lonchura hunsteini) is a species of estrildid finch breeding in New Ireland. This species is also introduced to Pohnpei. It has an estimated global extent of occurrence of 20,000 to 50,000 km2. It is found in subtropical/ tropical (lowland) dry grassland habitat. The New Hanover mannikin has sometimes been treated as a subspecies of mottled mannikin with the name Hunstein's mannikin for the combined taxa. The status of mottled mannikin (with New Hanover mannikin included) is evaluated as Least Concern. The males are similarly colored to the extinct Hawaiian Ula Ai Hāwane, a Hawaiian honeycreeper.

children.name: Lonchura forbesi
children.description: Forbes's mannikin (Lonchura forbesi) or the New Ireland munia, is a species of estrildid finch breeding in Papua New Guinea. It has an estimated global extent of occurrence. It is found in subtropical or tropical lowland dry grassland habitat. The status of the species is evaluated as Least Concern.

children.name: Lonchura nigerrima
children.description: New Hanover mannikin (Lonchura nigerrima) is a species of estrildid finch breeding in New Hannover. It has an estimated global extent of occurrence of 20,000 to 50,000 km2. It is found in subtropical/ tropical (lowland) dry grassland habitat. The New Hanover mannikin has sometimes been treated as a subspecies of Mottled mannikin. The status of Mottled mannikin (with New Hanover mannikin included) is evaluated as Least Concern.

children.name: Lonchura flaviprymna
children.description: The yellow-rumped mannikin (Lonchura flaviprymna) also known as the yellow-rumped munia, is a species of estrildid finch found in the eastern Kimberley region and north-west Northern Territory, Australia. It has an estimated global extent of occurrence of 20,000 to 50,000 km2. It is found in subtropical to tropical mangrove, moist savanna and wetland habitats. The conservation status of the species is evaluated as being of Least Concern.

children.name: Lonchura monticola
children.description:
The eastern alpine mannikin (Lonchura monticola) or alpine munia is a species of estrildid finch native to the Papuan Peninsula. It has an estimated global extent of occurrence of 20,000 to 50,000 km2.
It is found in subtropical/ tropical high altitude grassland habitat. The status of the species is evaluated as Least Concern.

children.name: Lonchura mela
children.description: A small munia with black wings, brown body, and white belly. It is found in grasslands of the Lesser Sunda Islands.

children.name: Lonchura pectoralis
children.description: A munia with a black face and bib, white breast with dark scaling, brown back, and black belly. It is found in dry grasslands of northern Australia.

children.name: Lonchura cucullata
children.description: The bronze mannikin or bronze munia (Spermestes cucullata) is a small passerine (i.e.

children.name: Lonchura fringilloides
children.description: The magpie mannikin or magpie munia (Spermestes fringilloides) is a species of estrildid finch, sparsely present across Sub-Saharan Africa.

children.name: Amadina
children.description: The cut-throat and related finches — a small genus of African estrildids with stout cones and distinctive throat patterns. The Cut-throat Finch is named for the male's vivid red throat band that resembles a wound. These are birds of dry savannas and scrublands, often gathering at waterholes in large numbers. They build untidy grass nests in trees or bushes, often reusing old weaver nests.

children.name: Amadina fasciata
children.description: The cut-throat finch (Amadina fasciata) is a common species of estrildid finch found throughout Africa; it is also known as the bearded finch, the ribbon finch, the cut throat, and the weaver finch.

children.name: Amadina erythrocephala
children.description:
The red-headed finch (Amadina erythrocephala) (also known as the paradise finch) is a common species of estrildid finch found in Africa. It has an estimated global extent of occurrence. It is found in Angola, Botswana, Lesotho, Namibia, South Africa and Zimbabwe.
Males have vibrant red heads and chests while the females are duller. The resemblance to the cut-throat finch is unmistakable. The red-headed and cut-throat finch are the only members of the genus Amadina. Amadinas with their heavy beaks resemble members of the Lonchura, so they are actually more closely related to the Pytilias such as the Melba finch.

children.name: Amandava
children.description: The avadavats — a small genus of brilliantly plumaged Asian estrildids with striking red breeding plumage in males. They are among the most colourful small passerines in Asia, with the male Red Avadavat covered in tiny white spots set against a red background. They frequent tall grasslands and wetlands, building domed grass nests with a side entrance.

children.name: Amandava amandava
children.description: The red avadavat (Amandava amandava), red munia or strawberry finch, is a sparrow-sized bird of the family Estrildidae.

children.name: Amandava formosa
children.description: The green avadavat or green munia (Amandava formosa) is a species of Estrildid finch with green and yellow on the body, a bright red bill and black "zebra stripes" on the flanks.

children.name: Amandava subflava
children.description:
The orange-breasted waxbill (Amandava subflava), also known as the zebra waxbill, is a small (approximately 9 cm long) sparrow-like bird with a reddish iris, orange breast, red bill and dark olive-green plumage. The male has a red rump, dark bars on the whitish flank and a scarlet eyebrow stripe. The female is duller and smaller than male; it also lacks the male's red eyebrow.
The orange-breasted waxbill is found in grassland and savannahs south of the Sahara in Africa. It has an estimated global extent of occurrence of 10,000,000 km2. This species is also introduced to other countries, e.g., Kuwait. Its diet consists mainly of seeds, insects and shoots. The female usually lays between four and six eggs in an oval-shaped nest made from grass. These nests are often the old nests of red-collared widowbirds.

children.name: Uraeginthus
children.description: The blue waxbills — a small genus of strikingly coloured African estrildids with brilliant blue faces, throats, and underparts. These delicate, fine-billed seedeaters are among the most beautiful African finches, occurring across savanna and woodland habitats. They are active, cheerful birds, often seen in pairs or small flocks at the edges of woodlands and in gardens.

children.name: Uraeginthus angolensis
children.description: The blue waxbill (Uraeginthus angolensis), also called southern blue waxbill, blue-breasted waxbill, southern cordon-bleu, blue-cheeked cordon-bleu, blue-breasted cordon-bleu and Angola cordon-bleu, is a common species of estrildid finch found in Southern Africa.

children.name: Uraeginthus bengalus
children.description: The red-cheeked cordon-bleu or red-cheeked cordonbleu (Uraeginthus bengalus) is a small passerine bird in the family Estrildidae. This estrildid finch is a resident breeding bird in drier regions of tropical Sub-Saharan Africa. Red-cheeked cordon-bleu has an estimated global extent of occurrence of 7,700,000 km2.

children.name: Uraeginthus cyanocephalus
children.description: The blue-capped cordon-bleu or blue-capped cordonbleu (Uraeginthus cyanocephalus) is native to Ethiopia, Kenya, Somalia, South Sudan, and Tanzania in East Africa. This small finch does fairly well in captivity given adequate conditions; however, breeding this finch is said to be quite difficult.

children.name: Brunhilda
children.description: A small genus of African waxbills with distinctive black, white, and red facial patterns. They were formerly included in Estrilda but are distinguished by their heavier bills and striking black-and-red facial masks. They inhabit dry savanna and thorn scrub across eastern and southern Africa.

children.name: Brunhilda erythronotos
children.description: The black-faced waxbill (Brunhilda erythronotos) is a common species of estrildid finch found in southern Africa. It is found in Angola, Botswana, Kenya, Namibia, Rwanda, South Africa, Tanzania, Uganda, Zambia and Zimbabwe. The IUCN has classified the species as being of least concern.

children.name: Spermophaga
children.description: The bluebills — a small genus of large, robust estrildids with heavy blue-grey bills adapted for cracking hard seeds. They are found in forests and dense thickets across tropical Africa. Males are strikingly coloured with red, black, and white plumage, while females are duller. They are shy, retiring birds that forage on the forest floor.

children.name: Spermophaga ruficapilla
children.description:
The red-headed bluebill (Spermophaga ruficapilla) is a common species of estrildid finch found in Sub-Saharan Africa.
It is found in Angola, Burundi, Central African Republic, The Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kenya, Rwanda, South Sudan, Tanzania and Uganda.

children.name: Spermophaga poliogenys
children.description:
Grant's bluebill (Spermophaga poliogenys) is a species of estrildid finch found in forests in central Africa in subtropical forests or in moist lowlands. It has an estimated global extent of occurrence of 350,000 km2.
It is found in the Republic of Congo, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda. The IUCN has classified the species as being of least concern.

children.name: Spermophaga haematina
children.description: The western bluebill (Spermophaga haematina) is a common species of estrildid finch found in Africa.

children.name: Mandingoa
children.description: A monotypic genus of African estrildid containing the Green Twinspot. It is a beautifully coloured finch of lowland and montane forests, with a glittering spotted breast that gives it its name. Its iridescent green spots are unique among African waxbills.

children.name: Mandingoa nitidula
children.description: The green-backed twinspot or green twinspot (Mandingoa nitidula) is an estrildid finch found in many parts of Sub-Saharan Africa. The IUCN has classified the species as being of least concern.

children.name: Lagonosticta
children.description: The firefinches — a genus of small, beautifully coloured African estrildids named for the brilliant crimson and pink plumage of the males. They are among the most vividly coloured small birds in Africa, with females being duller brownish versions. They inhabit savanna, scrub, and forest edges, often near water, and build domed grass nests with a side entrance.

children.name: Lagonosticta senegala
children.description: The red-billed firefinch or Senegal firefinch (Lagonosticta senegala) is a small seed-eating bird in the family Estrildidae. This is a resident breeding bird in most of Sub-Saharan Africa with an estimated global extent of occurrence of 10,000,000 km2. It was introduced to Egypt, but the population there has become extinct. It was also introduced to southern Algeria where it is currently expanding northward.

children.name: Lagonosticta rubricata
children.description: The African firefinch (Lagonosticta rubricata), also called the blue-billed firefinch, is a common species of estrildid finch found in many parts of Africa.

children.name: Lagonosticta rhodopareia
children.description: Jameson's firefinch (Lagonosticta rhodopareia) is a common species of estrildid finch, sparsely spread across sub-Saharan Africa. It has an estimated global extent of occurrence of 2,600,000 km2.

children.name: Lagonosticta rufopicta
children.description: The bar-breasted firefinch (Lagonosticta rufopicta) is a common species of estrildid finch found in western and central Africa. It has an estimated global extent of occurrence of 2,900,000 km².

children.name: Lagonosticta nitidula
children.description: The brown firefinch (Lagonosticta nitidula) is a common species of estrildid finch found in Southern Africa.

children.name: Lagonosticta landanae
children.description: The African firefinch (Lagonosticta rubricata), also called the blue-billed firefinch, is a common species of estrildid finch found in many parts of Africa.

children.name: Lagonosticta virata
children.description: The Mali firefinch (Lagonosticta virata) is a species of estrildid finch found in Western Africa.

children.name: Lagonosticta sanguinodorsalis
children.description: The rock firefinch (Lagonosticta sanguinodorsalis) is a species of estrildid finch found in the Jos Plateau of central Nigeria and in Cameroon.

children.name: Lagonosticta umbrinodorsalis
children.description: The Chad firefinch or Reichenow's firefinch (Lagonosticta umbrinodorsalis) is a small passerine bird belonging to the firefinch genus Lagonosticta in the estrildid finch family Estrildidae.

children.name: Granatina
children.description: A small genus of spectacular African estrildids noted for their brilliant violet, blue, and chestnut plumage. The Violet-eared Waxbill and Purple Grenadier are among the most beautiful of all African finches, with males displaying an extraordinary array of iridescent colours. They inhabit dry savanna and thorn scrub.

children.name: Granatina granatina
children.description: The violet-eared waxbill or common grenadier (Granatina granatina) is a common species of estrildid finch found in drier land of Southern Africa.

children.name: Granatina ianthinogaster
children.description: The purple grenadier (Granatina ianthinogaster) is a common species of estrildid finch found in eastern Africa.

children.name: Coccopygia
children.description: A small genus of African waxbills with yellow or greenish underparts and distinctive red rumps. They are among the smallest estrildids, with delicate bills and active, acrobatic feeding habits. They inhabit montane grasslands, forest edges, and cultivated areas in eastern and southern Africa.

children.name: Coccopygia quartinia
children.description:
The yellow-bellied waxbill (Coccopygia quartinia) is a species of estrildid finch native to East Africa. The bird is now named yellow-bellied swee.
It breeds in east central and south-eastern Africa. Some taxonomists consider it to be conspecific with the swee waxbill.

children.name: Coccopygia melanotis
children.description: The swee waxbill (Coccopygia melanotis), is a common species of estrildid finch native to Southern Africa.

children.name: Pyrenestes
children.description: The seedcrackers — a small genus of African estrildids with massively thick, powerful bills adapted for cracking the hardest seeds. They exhibit a remarkable polymorphism in bill size, with two distinct morphs occurring within the same population. They inhabit forests and dense thickets.

children.name: Pyrenestes sanguineus
children.description: The crimson seedcracker (Pyrenestes sanguineus) is a common species of estrildid finch found in Africa.

children.name: Pyrenestes ostrinus
children.description: The black-bellied seedcracker (Pyrenestes ostrinus) is a bird species of the family Estrildidae. They live in most Central African countries and inhabit tropical rainforest. The species comprises individuals with different physical appearance which are grouped into three categories (small, large and mega bill size). Adults are mainly granivorous but diet preference varies with bill size and food availability. Black-bellied seedcrackers also exhibit very distinctive colorations with bright patches of black and red, making them easy to identify in the field. Overall, little is known about this species apart from its range, but intensive studies are currently looking at bill size variations among individuals and their effects on behaviors.

children.name: Pyrenestes minor
children.description: The lesser seedcracker or Nyasa seedcracker (Pyrenestes minor) is a fairly common species of estrildid finch found in eastern Africa.

children.name: Pytilia
children.description: The pytilias — a genus of colourful African estrildids with green or red wings and finely barred underparts. They are active, often confiding birds of savanna and woodland edges. Their flight is fast and direct with a characteristic whirring sound.

children.name: Pytilia melba
children.description: The green-winged pytilia (Pytilia melba) is a small colourful seed-eating bird in the family Estrildidae. It is widespread throughout Sub-Saharan Africa, though it is more rarely seen in central, far southern and coastal western parts of the continent.

children.name: Pytilia afra
children.description: The orange-winged pytilia (Pytilia afra), also known as the golden-backed pytilia, is a species of estrildid finch found in Africa. It has a wide range and the International Union for Conservation of Nature has assessed it as being of least concern.

children.name: Pytilia phoenicoptera
children.description:
The red-winged pytilia (Pytilia phoenicoptera) is a common species of estrildid finch found in Africa. It has an estimated global extent of occurrence.
It is found at Benin, Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Central African Republic, Chad, The Democratic Republic of the Congo, Côte d'Ivoire, Ethiopia, Gambia, Ghana, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Mali, Niger, Nigeria, Senegal, Sierra Leone, Sudan, Togo and Uganda. The IUCN has classified the species as being of least concern.

children.name: Pytilia hypogrammica
children.description: The yellow-winged pytilia (Pytilia hypogrammica), also known as the red-faced pytilia, is an African estrildid finch.

children.name: Cryptospiza
children.description: The crimson-wings — a small genus of shy, forest-dwelling African estrildids with red wings, olive-green bodies, and dark faces. They are secretive birds of montane forest undergrowth, often difficult to observe as they forage quietly in deep shade.

children.name: Cryptospiza shelleyi
children.description: Shelley's crimsonwing (Cryptospiza shelleyi) is a vulnerable species of estrildid finch native to the Albertine Rift montane forests. It has shown population decline over the past few decades, with a current population estimate of 1,000–2,499. This is possibly related to uncontrolled deforestation.

children.name: Cryptospiza jacksoni
children.description: The dusky crimsonwing (Cryptospiza jacksoni) is a common species of estrildid finch found in Africa.

children.name: Cryptospiza salvadorii
children.description: The Abyssinian crimsonwing (Cryptospiza salvadorii), also known as the Ethiopian crimsonwing, Salvadori's crimsonwing or crimson-backed forest finch, is a common species of estrildid finch found in eastern Africa.

children.name: Cryptospiza reichenovii
children.description:
The red-faced crimsonwing (Cryptospiza reichenovii) is a common species of estrildid finch found in Africa. It has an estimated global extent of occurrence of 390,000 km2.
It is native to subsaharan mountainous regions: Bioko and the Western High Plateau, the Albertine Rift montane forests and east Africa (from northern Tanzania to eastern Zimbabwe).

children.name: Hypargos
children.description: The twinspots — a small genus of beautifully patterned African estrildids with spotted breasts and bright rumps. They are shy, retiring birds of forest undergrowth and dense thickets, often more easily heard than seen. Their melodious calls are characteristic sounds of African forests.

children.name: Hypargos niveoguttatus
children.description:
The red-throated twinspot (Hypargos niveoguttatus) or Peters's twinspot is a common species of bird found in sub-saharan Africa. This species has a large range, with an estimated global extent of occurrence.
It is commonly seen in Angola, Burundi, The Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kenya, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, Rwanda, Somalia, South Africa, Tanzania, Zambia & Zimbabwe. The status of the species is evaluated as Least Concern.

children.name: Hypargos margaritatus
children.description: The pink-throated twinspot (Hypargos margaritatus) is a small seed-eating bird in the family Estrildidae. It inhabits dry savanna and moist, subtropical/tropical (lowland) shrubland habitats near the southeast African coast in Mozambique, South Africa and Eswatini. It has a large range, with an estimated global extent of occurrence of 160,000 km2.

children.name: Euschistospiza
children.description: A small genus of African estrildids related to the twinspots, with finely spotted breasts and rich maroon or dusky plumage. They are shy, secretive birds of montane and lowland forests, foraging on the ground in dense cover.

children.name: Euschistospiza dybowskii
children.description:
Dybowski's twinspot (Euschistospiza dybowskii) is a common species of estrildid finch found in Africa. It has an estimated global extent of occurrence of 450,000 km2.
It is found in Cameroon, Central African Republic, Chad, The Democratic Republic of the Congo, Côte d'Ivoire, Guinea, Liberia, Nigeria, Senegal, Sierra Leone, South Sudan and Uganda. The status of the species is evaluated as Least Concern.

children.name: Euschistospiza cinereovinacea
children.description: The dusky twinspot (Euschistospiza cinereovinacea) is a species of estrildid finch found in Sub-Saharan Africa.

children.name: Nigrita
children.description: The negrofinches — a genus of African estrildids with contrasting black, grey, and white plumage, found in forests and woodlands across sub-Saharan Africa. They are active, acrobatic birds that forage in the canopy and understory, often in mixed-species flocks.

children.name: Nigrita bicolor
children.description: The chestnut-breasted nigrita (Nigrita bicolor) is a common species of estrildid finch found in Africa. It has an estimated global extent of occurrence of 3,000,000 km2.

children.name: Nigrita luteifrons
children.description:
The pale-fronted nigrita (Nigrita luteifrons) is a common species of estrildid finch found in Africa. It has an estimated global extent of occurrence of 2,500,000 km2.
It is widespread throughout the African tropical rainforest (although more sparsely throughout the Upper Guinean forests).

children.name: Nigrita canicapilla
children.description:
The grey-headed nigrita (Nigrita canicapillus) is a common species of estrildid finch found in Africa. It has an estimated global extent of occurrence of 3,700,000 km2.
It is widespread throughout the African tropical rainforest.

children.name: Nigrita fusconota
children.description:
The white-breasted nigrita (Nigrita fusconotus) is a very small nigrita with a rather waxbill-like appearance, a black cap and tail contrast with a brown back and wings and white under parts. Both sexes are alike but the immature has the crown, rump and tail browner.
It is widespread throughout the African tropical rainforest. It has an estimated global extent of occurrence of 2,700,000 km2.

children.name: Nesocharis
children.description: The olivebacks — a small genus of African estrildids with olive-green and grey plumage, thick bills, and a distinctive white collar. They are found in forests and montane scrub of West and Central Africa, where they forage quietly in the canopy for seeds and small fruits.

children.name: Nesocharis ansorgei
children.description:
The white-collared oliveback (Nesocharis ansorgei) is a species of estrildid finch found in Africa. It has an estimated global extent of occurrence of 94,000 km2.
It could be found at Burundi, The Democratic Republic of the Congo, Rwanda, Tanzania & Uganda. However, it is not commonly seen in at least parts of its range. The IUCN has classified the species as being of least concern.

children.name: Nesocharis shelleyi
children.description:
Shelley's oliveback (Nesocharis shelleyi), also known as the Fernando Po oliveback, is a species of estrildid finch found in Africa. It has an estimated global extent of occurrence of 55,000 km2.
It is found in Bioko island, western Cameroon and adjacent Nigeria. The IUCN has classified the species as being of least concern.

children.name: Parmoptila
children.description: The antpeckers — a small genus of African estrildids with finely spotted plumage and a unique association with ants. They are named for their habit of following ant columns to feed on insects flushed by the ants, a behaviour unusual among estrildids. They have stout, rather finch-like bills.

children.name: Parmoptila rubrifrons
children.description: The red-fronted antpecker (Parmoptila rubrifrons) is a species of songbird found in Western Africa. Like all antpeckers, it is placed in the estrildid finch family, Estrildidae. Jameson's antpecker (P. Jamesoni) has sometimes been considered as a subspecies.

children.name: Parmoptila jamesoni
children.description:
Jameson's antpecker (Parmoptila jamesoni) is a songbird species found in central Africa. Like all antpeckers, it is tentatively placed in the estrildid finch family (Estrildidae). It has traditionally been included as a subspecies of P. Rubrifrons (red-fronted antpecker) and the common name Jameson's antpecker was sometimes used for both taxa. But today, they are often considered distinct species.
Jameson's antpecker inhabits tropical lowland moist forest in Uganda, Tanzania and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. When Jameson's and the red-fronted antpeckers were still evaluated as one species, they were classified as a species of least concern by the IUCN. Unlike its western relative which is declining noticeably, P. Jamesoni is still common and widespread. Therefore, its status has not changed after its elevation to a full species.

children.name: Parmoptila woodhousei
children.description: Woodhouse's antpecker (Parmoptila woodhousei) is a species of passerine bird found in West Africa that is placed in the estrildid finch family, Estrildidae. The name commemorates the American explorer and collector Samuel Washington Woodhouse.

children.name: Paludipasser
children.description: A monotypic genus of African estrildid containing the Locust Finch, a small, secretive bird of wetlands and moist grasslands. It is named for its preference for grasshopper and locust nymphs, which supplement its seed-based diet. It is one of the most elusive of the African waxbills.

children.name: Paludipasser locustellus
children.description: A tiny finch with brown upperparts, a red face and rump, and pale underparts. It is found in moist grasslands and marshes of Central and East Africa, often near water.

children.name: Ortygospiza
children.description: The quailfinches — a small genus of terrestrial estrildids resembling miniature quail in their shape and ground-dwelling habits. They are found in moist grasslands and marshes across Africa, where they forage on the ground for grass seeds. Their short, rounded wings and strong legs reflect their largely terrestrial lifestyle.

children.name: Ortygospiza atricollis
children.description: The black-faced quailfinch (Ortygospiza atricollis atricollis), is a common subspecies of estrildid finch found in western and central of Africa. Some taxonomists consider it to be conspecific with the African quailfinch, others consider all three species to be conspecific.

children.name: Ortygospiza fuscocrissa
children.description: The African quailfinch, spectacled quailfinch, or white-chinned quailfinch (Ortygospiza atricollis fuscocrissa), is a common species of estrildid finch found in eastern and southern Africa.

children.name: Ortygospiza gabonensis
children.description: The black-chinned quailfinch (Ortygospiza atricollis gabonensis) also known as the red-billed quailfinch, is a common subspecies of estrildid finch found in central Africa. It has an estimated global extent of occurrence of 450,000 km2. It is found in Angola, Burundi, the Republic of Congo, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Equatorial Guinea, Gabon, Rwanda, Tanzania and Zambia. The IUCN has classified the species as being of least concern. Some taxonomists consider it to be conspecific with the other species of quailfinch.

children.name: Amurestes
children.description: A genus of African estrildids with distinctive black, red, and white plumage patterns. The Crimson Seedcracker and related species have massively developed bills for cracking hard seeds.

children.name: Amurestes obscurus
children.description: A finch with a red face, dark brown upperparts, and grey underparts. It is found in forests of Central Africa.

children.name: Sporaeginthus
children.description: A small genus of African estrildids known as the seedeaters or cordon-bleus, with bright blue plumage on the face and underparts. They are among the most beautiful of the small African finches.

children.name: Emblema
children.description: A monotypic genus of Australian estrildid containing the Painted Finch, a strikingly coloured bird of rocky hillsides and arid scrublands. It is named for its brilliant red and black facial pattern that resembles painted markings.

children.name: Emblema pictum
children.description: The painted finch (Emblema pictum) is a common species of estrildid finch found in Australia.

children.name: Stagonopleura
children.description: The firetails — a genus of Australian estrildids with brilliant crimson rumps and tails, found in coastal and forested regions of Australia. They are plump, active finches with distinctive black-and-white patterns on the face and throat.

children.name: Stagonopleura guttata
children.description: The diamond firetail (Stagonopleura guttata) is a species of estrildid finch that is endemic to Australia.

children.name: Stagonopleura bella
children.description: The beautiful firetail (Stagonopleura bella) is a common species of estrildid finch found in Australia.

children.name: Stagonopleura oculata
children.description:
The red-eared firetail (Stagonopleura oculata), also known as the boorin, is a small finch-like species of bird. It occurs in dense wetland vegetation of coastal to sub-coastal regions in Southwest Australia. Its appearance is considered appealing, with white spots, black barring and vivid crimson marks at the ear and upper tail. Red-eared firetails are usually only glimpsed briefly, if at all, as they move rapidly and discreetly through their habitat. Most observations occur when their soft voice is heard, or in flight when flushed from the dense scrub. Males and females are similar in colouring and bond as lifelong pairs that occupy a territory centred on their roosting and brooding nest site. The species occupies a similar ecological niche to the beautiful firetail (Stagonopleura bella) found in the east of Australia, although unlike other species of the genus they only occasionally group together and are almost never seen in large flocks.
The red-eared firetail is rare in captivity, being neither recommended nor generally permitted, as they require expertise and a large specialised environment to maintain their secretive habits; however, the observations in avicultural literature have supported and contributed to knowledge of its behaviour. Despite their shyness toward other birds and people, they are known to be less so when venturing out to bird feeders. The species is not easily confused with other birds in its native habitat, excepting perhaps the red-browed finch (Neochmia temporalis) that has escaped captivity and bred in the region.

children.name: Neochmia
children.description: A genus of Australian estrildids with brilliant red markings on the face and rump, found in grasslands and woodlands across Australia. They are lively, active finches that often gather in large flocks.

children.name: Neochmia temporalis
children.description:
The red-browed finch (Neochmia temporalis) is an estrildid finch native to the east coast of Australia. This species has established introduced populations near Perth and in the Darling Ranges, and is also feral in French Polynesia. It is commonly found in temperate forest and dry savannah habitats. It may also be found in dry forest and mangrove habitats in tropical regions.
The species is distinguished by the bright red stripe above the eye and bright red rump. The rest of the body is grey, with olive wing coverts and collar. Juveniles do not have red brow marks and lack olive colouration on the collar and wing coverts. The adults are long.

children.name: Neochmia ruficauda
children.description: The star finch (Emblema ruficauda) is a seed-eating bird species found in northern Australia.

children.name: Poephila
children.description: The grassfinches — a genus of long-tailed Australian estrildids with black bibs and chestnut or grey plumage. They are birds of arid and semi-arid grasslands, often seen in large flocks drinking at waterholes.

children.name: Poephila acuticauda
children.description: The long-tailed finch (Poephila acuticauda) is a common species of estrildid finch found in northern Australia, from the Kimberley region to the Gulf of Carpentaria. It is a predominantly fawn-coloured bird with a pale grey head and prominent black bib and eyes. It inhabits dry savannah habitats in Australia and adapts readily to aviculture. It is known as the Hex finch in the United Kingdom, and Heck's finch in other parts of the world.

children.name: Poephila cincta
children.description: The black-throated finch (Poephila cincta), or parson finch, is a species of estrildid finch found in grassy woodlands throughout north-east Australia from Cape York Peninsula to central Queensland. The southern black-throated finch (Poephila cincta cincta) is endangered, with a population in decline and its habitat is threatened by development, and has become extinct in New South Wales, while the northern black-throated finch (Poephila cincta atropygialis) is not listed as threatened at this point.

children.name: Poephila personata
children.description: The masked finch (Poephila personata) is a small passerine bird in the estrildid finch family, Estrildidae.

children.name: Heteromunia
children.description: A monotypic genus of Australian estrildid containing the Pictorella Munia, a distinctive finch with a scaly white breast and a blue-grey bill. It is found in dry grasslands of northern Australia.

children.name: Heteromunia pectoralis
children.description: The pictorella mannikin, pictorella munia, or pictorella finch (Heteromunia pectoralis) is small brown and grey finch with a grey bill and distinctive scaly white breast plate which is endemic to northern Australia.

children.name: Odontospiza
children.description: A monotypic genus of African estrildid containing the Crimson-rumped Waxbill, a small finch with a bright red rump and distinctive facial markings. It is found in dry savannas of East Africa.

children.name: Odontospiza griseicapilla
children.description: The grey-headed silverbill (Spermestes griseicapilla), also known as pearl-headed mannikin, is a species of estrildid finch found in eastern Africa, Ethiopia, Kenya, South Sudan, and Tanzania. It has an estimated global extent of occurrence. It was formerly usually placed in the monotypic genus Odontospiza as Odontospiza caniceps and sometimes placed in the genus Lonchura.

children.name: Glaucopectus
children.description: A genus of African estrildids with distinctive blue-grey bills and finely patterned plumage, found in savannas and woodlands of Africa.

children.name: Glaucopectus angolensis
children.description: A small waxbill with a blue-grey bill, brown upperparts, pale underparts, and a red rump. It is found in savannas of southwestern Africa.

children.name: Estrildopas
children.description: A small genus of African estrildids with black, white, and rufous plumage patterns, found in forests of Central Africa.

children.name: Estrildopas ruficeps
children.description: A waxbill with a rufous crown, black face, olive upperparts, and pale underparts. It is found in lowland forests of Central Africa.

children.name: Madagascara
children.description: A genus of estrildids endemic to Madagascar, with olive, yellow, and red plumage. They inhabit forests and scrub across the island.

children.name: Madagascara madagascariensis
children.description: A small finch with brown upperparts, white underparts, and a black face and throat. It is endemic to Madagascar, inhabiting grasslands and forests.

children.name: Madagascara nana
children.description: A tiny finch with brown upperparts, pale underparts, and a short tail. It is endemic to Madagascar, inhabiting grasslands and wetlands.

children.name: Carpophaga
children.description: A genus of Pacific island estrildids with thick bills and brown, black, and white plumage. They are found on islands of the southwest Pacific.

children.name: Carpophaga melanura
children.description: A stocky munia with a black tail, brown upperparts, white underparts, and a thick grey bill. It is found on islands of Fiji and Tonga.

children.name: Carpophaga pectoralis
children.description: A munia with a white breast, brown upperparts, black belly, and thick bill. It is found on islands of Vanuatu and New Caledonia.

children.name: Calliphthalmus
children.description: A genus of African estrildids with bright red or orange bills and colourful plumage, found in savannas and woodlands.

children.name: Calliphthalmus erythrothorax
children.description: A waxbill with a red breast, brown upperparts, and a red bill. It is found in savannas of West Africa.

children.name: Calliphthalmus rubriventris
children.description: A waxbill with a red belly, brown upperparts, and a red bill. It is found in savannas of central Africa.

children.name: Calliphthalmus flaviventris
children.description: A waxbill with a yellow belly, brown upperparts, and a red bill. It is found in savannas of southern Africa.

children.name: Calliphthalmus nigrimentum
children.description: A waxbill with a black chin, brown upperparts, and pale underparts. It is found in savannas of East Africa.

children.name: Entomophaga
children.description: A genus of insectivorous estrildids found in the forests of Central Africa, with olive and yellow plumage and fine bills adapted for catching small insects.

children.name: Entomophaga insectivora
children.description: A small waxbill with olive upperparts, yellow underparts, and a fine black bill. It is found in lowland forests of central Africa.

children.name: Entomophaga chloropoda
children.description: A waxbill with green legs, olive upperparts, and yellow underparts. It is found in montane forests of East Africa.

children.name: Entomophaga flaviventris
children.description: A small finch with bright yellow underparts, olive upperparts, and a thin bill. It is found in forests of central Africa.
